blocks.text: Name: Foley urinary catheter (indwelling urinary catheter).
Classification: A flexible tube inserted through the urethra into the urinary bladder and retained by an inflatable balloon.
Distinguishing features:
A flexible shaft with drainage openings near its tip.
An inflatable retention balloon near the tip.
A drainage port that connects to a urine collection bag.
A balloon inflation port, usually with a valve.
A three-way Foley catheter has an additional port for bladder irrigation.

rows: Continuous bladder irrigation, particularly after selected urological procedures
Useful for some patients requiring longer-term catheterisation, including those with latex sensitivity if the product is confirmed latex-free
Selected difficult catheterisations, particularly with prostatic enlargement; requires appropriate training

blocks.text: Size: Catheters are measured in French gauge (Fr). Larger numbers indicate larger external diameters. Adult sizes commonly include 12–16 Fr, although the appropriate size depends on the indication, patient anatomy and local protocol. Smaller sizes are used in children.
Examiner identification statement:

“This is a Foley urinary catheter, an indwelling catheter retained in the bladder by an inflatable balloon. It is used for selected indications requiring continuous bladder drainage, urine-output monitoring or bladder irrigation.”
A Foley catheter should be inserted only when there is a clear clinical indication.
Acute urinary retention: To decompress the bladder when appropriate.
Accurate urine-output monitoring: Particularly in selected critically ill patients when hourly measurements will affect management.
Perioperative care: During selected operations or when specific postoperative monitoring is necessary.
Bladder irrigation: A three-way catheter may be used for continuous irrigation, such as in selected cases of haematuria with clots.
Selected urological procedures: When continuous drainage or access to the bladder is required.
Selected end-of-life care: When catheterisation improves comfort and aligns with the patient's goals.
Selected wound-care situations: When urine contamination would significantly impair healing and alternatives are unsuitable.

Important OSCE point: A Foley catheter is not routinely indicated simply because a patient is incontinent or because urine collection would be more convenient. Consider less invasive alternatives whenever appropriate.

blocks.text: Key distinction: The balloon retains the catheter; it does not drain urine. Urine drains through the drainage lumen.
Provides continuous bladder drainage.
Relieves urinary retention when appropriately indicated.
Allows accurate measurement of urine output in selected patients.
Can facilitate bladder irrigation when a suitable catheter is used.
May reduce repeated intermittent catheterisation in selected situations.
Can be useful during specific operations and postoperative care.

Urethral trauma, bleeding or creation of a false passage.
Discomfort, pain and bladder spasms.

Requires appropriate maintenance and regular review of the indication.
Exam pearl: The most important preventable risk is unnecessary catheterisation and unnecessarily prolonged catheter use.
Correct Foley catheter type and size.
Sterile catheterisation pack and sterile gloves.
Appropriate cleansing or antiseptic solution according to local protocol.
Sterile lubricant; local anaesthetic gel when indicated and appropriate.
Sterile water for balloon inflation, in the volume specified by the manufacturer.
Closed urine drainage bag and connecting tubing.
Waterproof protective sheet and receptacle for waste.
Specimen container, if a urine specimen is required.
Appropriate personal protective equipment.

Explain the procedure, obtain informed consent and offer a chaperone as appropriate.
Ask about allergies, particularly latex, antiseptics and lubricant ingredients.
Provide privacy and position the patient appropriately.

Maintain aseptic technique throughout insertion.

Balloon safety rule: Never inflate the balloon until the catheter is appropriately positioned within the bladder. Urine return is an important sign of placement, but the catheter must also be advanced sufficiently according to the device and local protocol.
Do not force the catheter against resistance. If there is significant pain, resistance, bleeding or concern about urethral injury, stop and seek experienced assistance.

subsections.subsection_title: How to use it — step-by-step practical demonstration

blocks.text: In an OSCE, verbalise consent, asepsis, patient comfort and balloon safety as you demonstrate.

Confirm identity and indication, explain the procedure, obtain consent, check allergies and provide privacy. Position the patient supine; a female patient may be placed in the dorsal recumbent position with knees flexed and legs apart.

items: Step 2 — Prepare equipment and maintain asepsis

blocks.text: Perform hand hygiene, arrange the sterile equipment, don sterile gloves and establish the sterile field. Prepare the catheter, lubricant and drainage system without contaminating sterile components.

Clean according to local policy, using the appropriate technique for the patient's anatomy. Maintain separation of the labia in a female patient or gently hold the penis appropriately in a male patient.
Apply adequate sterile lubricant; use anaesthetic gel when indicated and allow the recommended time for it to act.

Female: Separate the labia, identify the urethral opening and insert gently. If the catheter accidentally enters the vagina, leave it there temporarily as a landmark and use a new sterile catheter for the urethral attempt.
Male: Hold the penis gently, usually elevated to straighten the urethra, and advance the catheter slowly. Retract the foreskin if present and return it to its normal position afterwards.
Never force the catheter through resistance.
Wait for urine to drain. Advance the catheter further by the distance specified in the relevant protocol and appropriate to the patient's anatomy before inflating the balloon.

In a male patient, the catheter is generally advanced to the bifurcation or the appropriate insertion depth before balloon inflation. In a female patient, advance sufficiently beyond urine return according to local guidance.
Do not inflate the balloon merely because urine has appeared.
Inflate with the specified volume of sterile water through the balloon port, following the manufacturer's instructions.
Stop if inflation causes pain or resistance. Deflate the balloon and reassess placement; do not continue inflating against resistance.

Gently withdraw until the balloon rests at the bladder neck. Secure the catheter to minimise traction, connect to a closed drainage system and position the bag below bladder level and off the floor. Ensure the tubing is not kinked.

Ensure the patient is comfortable, dispose of waste safely and perform hand hygiene. Document the indication, catheter type and size, balloon volume, date and time, urine appearance and amount, any difficulties, and the ongoing plan for review and removal.
Keep the drainage system closed and maintain unobstructed urine flow.
Keep the bag below bladder level and off the floor.
Empty the bag using the designated outlet without contaminating it.
Obtain urine specimens from the designated sampling port using aseptic technique, not from the collection bag.
Review the indication daily and remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.
Do not routinely flush the catheter unless clinically indicated and authorised under the relevant protocol.

Suspected urethral injury is the key examination warning. If a patient has pelvic trauma with blood at the urethral meatus, perineal bruising or other signs suggesting urethral disruption, do not attempt blind urethral catheterisation. Obtain urgent senior/urological assessment; appropriate imaging and an alternative drainage route may be needed.
Other situations requiring caution or specialist input include:
Known or suspected urethral stricture.
Recent urethral or urological surgery.
Difficult previous catheterisation or suspected false passage.
An artificial urinary sphincter, which may require specific preparation by a trained clinician.
Relevant material allergy, such as latex allergy.

blocks.text: Examiner's question: What would you do if there is resistance during catheter insertion?

Model answer: “I would stop and never force the catheter. I would reassess the situation, provide reassurance and seek experienced or urological assistance if resistance persists or urethral injury is suspected.”
Urine drains freely through the catheter.
No significant pain or bleeding during insertion.
Tubing is unkinked and the drainage bag is below bladder level.
The catheter is secured without excessive traction.
The closed drainage system remains intact.
Urine colour and clarity should be documented when relevant, but neither cloudy urine nor an unpleasant smell alone confirms a urinary tract infection.

blocks.text: In acute care, urine output below approximately 0.5 mL/kg/hour is a commonly used threshold for oliguria in adults and children, but interpretation depends on age, duration, clinical context and the applicable criteria.
Safety point: Do not blindly flush a catheter or repeatedly attempt insertion when the cause of poor drainage is uncertain.
Use an age-appropriate catheter with the smallest suitable diameter that will achieve the clinical purpose.
Confirm balloon volume against the manufacturer's instructions; never assume an adult balloon volume is appropriate for a child.
Use adequate lubrication and gentle technique because the urethra is delicate.
Avoid repeated traumatic attempts. Seek an experienced clinician early in children with congenital urinary tract abnormalities, previous urethral surgery or suspected injury.
Use appropriate securement to prevent traction and accidental removal.
Maintain privacy, explain the procedure in developmentally appropriate language and involve a parent or guardian according to consent requirements and local policy.
Review the indication frequently and remove the catheter promptly when it is no longer needed.
Clean — prepare the patient and urethral meatus aseptically.
Lubricate — use adequate sterile lubricant.
Insert — gently, without forcing.
Urine — observe urine return as a placement sign.
Advance — sufficiently before balloon inflation.
Balloon — inflate with the specified sterile water volume only after appropriate placement.

content_groups.group_title: B. Drainage bag rule: “Below, Closed, No Kinks”

blocks.text: Below: Keep the bag below bladder level.
Closed: Avoid unnecessary disconnection.
No kinks: Maintain unobstructed drainage.
Remember that urine return alone does not justify immediate balloon inflation. The catheter must be advanced appropriately first.

subsections.subsection_title: Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is a Foley catheter?
A flexible indwelling urinary catheter retained in the bladder by an inflatable balloon.
Q2. What is the difference between a two-way and a three-way Foley catheter?
A two-way catheter has drainage and balloon-inflation lumens. A three-way catheter has an additional irrigation lumen, commonly used for continuous bladder irrigation when indicated.
Q3. What is the French gauge system?
It measures the external diameter of the catheter. A higher French number indicates a larger diameter.
Q4. When should the retention balloon be inflated?
After appropriate intravesical placement has been established, with urine return and sufficient advancement according to the device instructions and local protocol.
Q5. What fluid is used to inflate the balloon?
The specified volume of sterile water, according to the manufacturer's instructions. Do not substitute saline unless the device instructions specifically permit it.
Q6. What do you do if you encounter resistance?
Stop and do not force the catheter. Reassess and obtain experienced assistance if resistance persists or injury is suspected.
Q7. What are the signs that urethral injury may be present?
Blood at the urethral meatus, perineal bruising, pelvic trauma or significant resistance during attempted insertion. Suspected injury requires urgent assessment rather than repeated blind attempts.
Q8. Where should the urine collection bag be positioned?
Below bladder level and off the floor, with tubing free of kinks.
Q9. How do you collect a urine specimen from a catheterised patient?
Use the designated sampling port with aseptic technique. Do not collect a diagnostic specimen from the drainage bag.
Q10. How can you reduce CAUTI risk?
Use a catheter only when indicated, insert it aseptically, maintain a closed drainage system, keep urine flowing freely and remove the catheter as soon as possible.
Q11. What would you do if the catheter is draining no urine?

Assess the patient and urine-output trend, check for kinks or compression, and consider obstruction, malposition or an empty bladder. Escalate if unresolved; do not blindly flush or reinflate the balloon.
Q12. When should a Foley catheter be removed?
As soon as the indication has resolved, according to the clinical plan and local protocol.

blocks.text: High-yield examiner tip: The three major safety points are do not catheterise when urethral injury is suspected, do not force insertion, and do not inflate the balloon prematurely.

blocks.text: Indwelling urinary catheter retained by an inflatable balloon.
Consent, aseptic technique, adequate lubrication, gentle insertion and appropriate placement before balloon inflation.
Suspected urethral injury — no blind catheterisation.

Bag below bladder level, closed system, no kinks and prompt catheter removal when no longer indicated.
